newsitem.title: USA: Fans flood Memphis for Elvis anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Fans flood Memphis for Elvis anniversary.

text.p: Elvis Presley fans flooded Memphis on Friday by the tens of thousands to mourn the 20th anniversary of his death and celebrate the rock n' roll memories he gave the world.
It was 20 years ago on Saturday that an ambulance crew answered an emergency call at 3764 Elvis Presley Boulevard.

Inside the house, a stone-sided, white columned southern mansion better known a Graceland, they found the street's namesake dead in his bedroom. He was 42, and investigators would conclude he died of a drug-induced heart attack.

An estimated 50,000 people -- the biggest crowd to gather in Memphis since Presley's funeral two decades ago -- have come to this steamy city by the muddy Mississippi River to relive old love songs, remember teen-age crushes and tell their children how Elvis put their legs to dancing.

Thousands planned to join an all-night candlelight vigil on Friday night until daybreak Saturday outside Graceland, facing the hillside where Presley, his parents and paternal grandmother are buried in a garden half-circled by trellaced Corinthian columns on one side and a kidney-shaped swimming pool on the other.
"The grave got me," said a man from San Francisco who gave his name only as Paul. "I've been an Elvis fan ever since I was a little kid. My babysitter used to play Evis for me."

He and a companion had just finished touring Graceland at sunset on Thursday, joining the 9 million visitors that its operator, Elvis Presley Enterprises, claims have walked through since Elvis died. It is said to be the second most heavily visited home in the United States. The first is the White House.
"Not only that, I learned that his father outlived him. I didn't know that," Paul said. "You read the gravestones and say 'Wow, his dad outlived him'."

His companion, who gave his name as "Spig," said he grew up in Oxford, Mississippi, 30 miles (48 km) from the town where Elvis was born. He said the tour touched him when he saw the clothes Elvis wore and watched videos of his performances. "You're just next to it," he said. "Look at all the other pop icons. Where is the 50,000-people vigil for them?"

The visitors shuffle past the graves in ghostly silence, listening to a taped audio tour plugged into their ears but rarely speaking a word to one another. A young woman with long blonde hair sits for a few moments near the graves, holding her grief-stricken face in her hands.

From around the world those who couldn't journey to Memphis to mark the day have sent flowers, trinkets, stuffed animals and posters. They are strewn across the graves and stand sentry up and down the walkways leading from the Meditation Garden, as the graveyard is called. Every few minutes a uniformed guard drives up in a golf cart and plants one or two more tributes.

Dolores, Linda and Polly, hometown not listed, have sent an evergreen wreath inset with a plastic miniature model of Graceland decorated for Christmas with a pink Cadillac like the one Elvis once owned parked outside.
Beth and Kathie from St. Louis, Missouri, chose a guitar, spray painted black with a message written in gold "20 years, 20 million tears."

"The Official Fan Club of Denmark" has sent a bank of red carnations imbedded with a cross of white ones. On the swimming pool fence is a towel-sized banner reading "Elvis - We thank you for the freedom you gave us -- Brazilian fans." From Berlin, Edelgard and Michael have dispatched a yellow and red heart with a color photo of Elvis in the center.

At the head of his gravestone is a knee-high bronzed obelisk imprinted "Paris Remembers Elvis," a tiny tricolor fixed to its tip. Fans from Austria, New Zealand, Belgium, Britain and a number of other nations are represented as well.

But the mood away from the gravesite is celebatory. Fans jam souvenir counters and restaurants, and music fills the air from a tent near the massive staging area where fans sometimes wait hours to take the mansion tour.
The Memphis Convention and Visitors Bureau estimated the death anniversary and events during the week leading up to it would pour $25 million into the local economy.

There are dozens of daily concerts, shows by Elvis imitators, boat rides and scholarly discussions spread across the city -- all about the young man from Mississippi who turned pop music upside down in the 1950s with a blend of blues, gospel, country and black music that became rock and roll.
